newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-FORMULA ONE CONSIDERING STOCK MARKET FLOAT.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-FORMULA ONE CONSIDERING STOCK MARKET FLOAT.

text.p: Formula One, the global Grand Prix motor racing business, is considering a stock market flotation that would make its British founder, Bernie Ecclestone, a billionaire, financial sources said on Sunday.
They confirmed the accuracy of British newspaper reports that the listing, planned for London and New York, could go ahead before the summer and raise as much as 4 billion.
But a spokesman for Salomon Brothers, the U.S. investment bank which is preparing the deal, said nothing had been finalised.
"Salomon Brothers are talking with Mr Ecclestone about a number of options for Formula One, including an initial public offering (of shares).
"No decision has been taken about structure, timing or valuation and it is premature to speculate on any of these aspects," the spokesman said.

The flotation would capitalise on investors' thirst for high-profile sports businesses in Britain, where Newcastle United is one of several top soccer clubs planning to join Manchester United and Tottenham Hotspur on the stock market.

"In terms of global popularity, brand recognition and television potential, I can't think of a more attractive sporting contract business to take to the public market," Christian Purslow, head of Salomon's media and communications business, told the Sunday Telegraph.
It said advisers had been working on the flotation for months, trying to sort out the complex web of contacts between Ecclestone, the racing teams and the track owners.
Ecclestone, a former second-hand car dealer, has built Formula One Promotions and Administration over the past 25 years into a global business.
Ecclestone, 65, still owns most of the company and the flotation would turn him overnight into one of Britain's wealthiest men, the papers said.
The 17 Grand Prix races each year, contested by 12 teams, are big television moneymakers, attracting an average 330 million viewers in more than 130 countries.
The British television rights to Formula One for the next five years were recently sold for 70 million pounds (112 million).
The first of this year's series, the Australian Grand Prix in Melbourne, was won earlier on Sunday by British driver David Coulthard.
The advent of digital broadcasting, which will increase the number of channels, is expected to boost the worldwide audience for Formula One even further.

"While Mr Ecclestone's age has to be a factor in his decision to go public, the money raised is needed to fund the move to digital broadcasting, which will require the buying of satellite transmission time," the Sunday Telegraph said.
